newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: European feeds stay calm on weather watch.
newsitem.headline: European feeds stay calm on weather watch.

text.p: The European meals and feeds trade is set to continue its U.S. weather-watch, with analysts expecting higher soymeal prices in store unless rain falls soon.

A hair-trigger Chicago futures market has been roiled in the past two weeks by reports -- and then counter reports -- of hot, dry weather in the key growing regions of the Midwest. Physical consumers here have had to sit back and watch.
"This is going to be a big problem if there's no sign of rain," said Arie van Dijk of statisticians Stigevo.
Forecasting November soybeans as high as seven dollars, he said his advice to clients was to choose their buying moment carefully and not to step in too far.
"Consumers are entering a very difficult autumn and winter. My advice is to buy any "rain correction" now but wait until around October before filling November/April cover," he said.
A key date on the horizon is the USDA crop report on August 12, when an even more bullish outlook could emerge, he said.

CBOT soybean futures ended official trade on Friday a shade lower in consolidation ahead of the weekend. Dry weather reports pushed November beans up 60 cents a bushel over the week but traders said a hint of rain could easily wash away any gains. August ended down six cents at $7.62 but was quoted another 10 cents higher on Monday Project A trade.
The physical market opened quietly in Europe on Monday, with sellers offering South American soymeal up to five dollars above Friday's levels. The high dollar was an extra brake on trade.
"Everybody is concentrating on nearby, hand-to-mouth deals -- it's nothing new for this time of the year," one trader said.
But the prospect of heated soymeal prices was offering hope to sellers of other proteins, with rapemeal, feed peas and sunmeal singled out as favourites by Stigevo's Van Dijk.
"We could see some cover for alternatives to soymeal but there is a problem for rapemeal which is attracting a big premium in local markets from October onwards," he said.
Feed peas were the particular bargain of the moment with buying expected from producers in France and Canada.

But despite the firm market forecast for soymeal, consumers will have to bite the bullet at some time as cover remains low. Van Dijk estimated that compounder coverage until April next year was as low as 20 percent for soymeal.
Coverage of up to 40 percent was noted for other products.
